entries.title: U.S. Senate (Special Election)
entries.summary: Filling the remainder of Marco Rubio's term after his resignation to become U.S. Secretary of State. Governor DeSantis appointed Ashley Moody to hold the seat in the interim; the winner of the November special election serves the remaining two years of the term.
entries.details: Ashley Moody won the Republican nomination with 80% of the vote, ahead of Chris Gleason (14%), Ernest Rivera (5%), and Neelam Perry (2%). Angie Nixon won the Democratic nomination with 56%, defeating Alex Vindman (44%). Moody and Nixon face off in November, along with one independent candidate.

entries.title: U.S. House, District 6
entries.summary: Putnam County's congressional seat. Redrawn district boundaries favor the Republican nominee heading into November. Incumbent Randy Fine and Democratic nominee Eric Yonce face off for the seat.
entries.details: Randy Fine won the Republican nomination with 57%, ahead of Dan Bilzerian (19%), Aaron Baker (13%), Charles Gambaro (10%), and Manuel Asensio (1%). Eric Yonce won a close four-way Democratic primary with 32%, ahead of Ronnie Murchinson-Rivera (27%), Steve Morgan (23%), and Robert Cooper II (18%). Fine and Yonce meet on the November ballot.

entries.title: Florida State Senate, District 8
entries.summary: Open seat; term-limited Sen. Tommy Wright is not running. Only one candidate qualified per party, so there is no primary in this race, it goes straight to the November ballot.
entries.details: General election: Rep. Jake Johansson (Republican), Judy Ngying (Democrat), Gabriel Jude Wozniak (Libertarian).

entries.title: Florida House, District 20
entries.summary: Putnam County's state House seat. The incumbent and his challenger each ran unopposed within their own party, so there is no primary, it goes straight to the November ballot.
entries.details: General election: Rep. Judson Sapp (Republican, incumbent) vs. Lee Butler (Democrat).

entries.title: Putnam County Commission, District 4
entries.summary: Putnam's most closely watched local primary. Incumbent Larry Harvey held off a challenger running on spending and animal-control accountability.
entries.details: Larry Harvey won the Republican nomination with 60%, defeating Joseph "Joey" Agner (40%). Harvey faces Joshua Florence (Democrat, firefighter running on expanding healthcare access) and Ronald Burckhard (No Party Affiliation) on the November ballot.

entries.title: Palatka Mayor-Commissioner
entries.summary: Nonpartisan race for the top elected office in the county seat. Karl Flagg, a former Palatka mayor, won an outright majority in the August primary, unseating incumbent Robbi Correa.
entries.details: Karl Flagg won with 58% of the vote, defeating incumbent Robbi Correa (23%), Constance Daniels (17%), and Tatyiana Henry Daniel (3%). Because Flagg cleared a majority outright, the race is decided and will not appear on the November ballot (pending confirmation that Palatka's charter doesn't require a runoff regardless).

entries.title: Palatka City Commissioner, Group 2
entries.summary: Nonpartisan race for one of Palatka's city commission seats.
entries.details: Candidates: James Norwood (former commissioner) vs. Jamaad C. Batts, Sr.

entries.title: Seventh Judicial Circuit Court, Group 26
entries.summary: Nonpartisan judicial race covering Flagler, Putnam, St. Johns, and Volusia counties. All registered voters, regardless of party, could vote in this race. Jeanne Stratis won a majority outright in August, so the race is decided and will not appear on the November ballot.
entries.details: Jeanne Stratis won with 61% of the vote, defeating Carleen Leffler (39%).

entries.title: Amendment 1: Changes to the Budget Stabilization Fund
entries.summary: Raises the cap on Florida's "rainy day fund" from 10% to 25% of general revenue, and requires an annual transfer into it (up to $750 million a year) unless the legislature votes to suspend it. Needs 60% approval to pass.
entries.details: Supporters say bigger reserves protect the state during recessions and disasters and can lower the state's borrowing costs. Opponents say locking up more general revenue leaves less available in a given year for schools, healthcare, and infrastructure.

entries.title: Amendment 2: Agriculture and Agritourism Property Tax Exemption
entries.summary: Exempts tangible personal property used in farming or agritourism, like tractors and harvest equipment, from property taxes. Needs 60% approval to pass.
entries.details: Intended to lower operating costs for Florida's agricultural sector. In Putnam County, where agriculture is a significant part of the local economy, this could mean real relief for farm operations, offset by a small reduction in the county's taxable property base.

entries.title: Amendment 3: Homestead Tax Exemptions, Property Assessments, and Spending Restrictions
entries.summary: The largest of the three amendments. Raises the non-school homestead exemption from $25,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 (then indexes it to inflation), caps annual assessment increases on non-homestead property at 5% instead of 10%, and restricts how local governments can spend remaining property tax revenue. Needs 60% approval to pass.
entries.details: New Florida residents (establishing residency after Dec. 31, 2026) get a smaller $50,000 exemption until they have lived in the state five years. State economists estimate the amendment would cut local government revenue statewide by close to $12 billion a year by 2031. For a county where median household income and home values both run well below the state average, a $250,000 exemption could remove a large share of residential property from the local tax base, which may push county and city governments toward new fees or reduced services to make up the difference.

entries.summary: These offices drew no qualified opposition and did not appear on the primary ballot. They were already elected or advanced automatically.
entries.details: County Commission District 2: Leota Wilkinson (R). School Board District 1: Holly Pickens. School Board District 4: Linda Wagner. School Board District 5: Phil Leary.
